opus-5.5.text:
I think Yann is a very pure scientist at heart. A lot of people know him from social media, where he's combative, very opinionated, and always arguing with someone. That's real, it's part of him. But when you work with him up close, what strikes you most is how consistent he is. He has believed certain things for decades, and he keeps pushing on them whether or not they're fashionable.

When neural networks were out of favor, he kept working on them. Now everyone is excited about large language models, and he's one of the loudest voices saying this isn't the full answer and that we need systems that understand the physical world, can plan, and have something like world models. You can agree or disagree, but he isn't saying it to be contrarian. It comes from a very coherent picture of what intelligence should be, one he's been refining for a long time.

On a personal level, he's surprisingly approachable. There's no sense of hierarchy with him. He'll talk to a first-year student the same way he talks to a senior researcher. He's curious about everything: music, building things, sailing, astronomy. He still gets excited about ideas like a young researcher. I find that inspiring, because in this field it's easy to get cynical or to just chase whatever trend is hot.

He's also very generous about letting people explore. He doesn't micromanage. He gives you a direction and a lot of freedom, and he trusts that good research comes from people following their own taste. I think that's shaped a lot of people who came through FAIR and NYU.

If I had to sum him up in one phrase, it would be "stubborn in a good way." He has strong convictions, and he's willing to be unpopular for them. History has shown that kind of stubbornness can be very valuable in science.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann is a very genuine person. I think that's the first thing that stands out when you actually work with him, as opposed to just seeing him on Twitter or in the news. He is extremely consistent. The things he says publicly are exactly the things he says in a one-on-one meeting or in a reading group. There's no gap between the public persona and the private one, which is rare for someone at that level of fame.

The second thing is that he's a true believer. He has been pushing the same set of ideas for decades, from convolutional nets in the eighties and nineties, when almost nobody cared, to self-supervised learning and world models today. People sometimes see that as stubbornness, but when you're close to it, it reads more like conviction. He really thinks about where the field should go in ten or twenty years rather than what will get a paper accepted next cycle. I was at FAIR for several years, and he never pressured anyone to chase the hot topic. He would tell you what he believed, argue with you if you disagreed, and then let you go do your own thing.

He's also quite generous with junior people. He treats a PhD student's argument the same way he treats a senior researcher's argument, meaning he will push back hard, but he's actually listening. Some of my most useful conversations with him were ones where we fundamentally disagreed. He enjoys the fight, intellectually, but it's never personal.

And he has a dry sense of humor that doesn't always come across online. In person he's warmer and funnier than his reputation suggests. I'd say he's a scientist first, in the old-fashioned sense, someone who cares about understanding how intelligence works more than about the products or the headlines. That's something I deeply respect, even on the questions where I think he might turn out to be wrong.
